Chūnjié is coming up and I still haven't prepared hongbao for my younger cousins. How would you handle that?

Don’t panic! It’s completely normal to feel rushed before Chūnjié, but there are **quick and practical solutions** to handle Hongbao last-minute. Here’s how to approach it: --- ### ✨ **Fastest & Easiest Solution: Digital Hongbaos (Highly Recommended!)** - **Why it works**: In modern times, ** digital Hongbaos via WeChat or Alipay are widely accepted** (especially for younger cousins). It’s instant, no physical envelopes needed, and many families now prefer this for convenience. - **Steps**: 1. Open WeChat/Alipay → "红包" (Hongbao) → "发红包" (Send Hongbao). 2. Choose the amount (e.g., **¥50, ¥100, or ¥200** per cousin— even numbers like 6, 8, or 10 are considered lucky; avoid "4" as it’s unlucky). 3. Add a festive message like "新年快乐！" (Happy New Year!) or "恭喜发财" (Wishing you prosperity). 4. **Send it immediately**— takes 2 minutes total. - **Why this is ideal**: No need to rush to stores, no worries about new bills, and it’s culturally appropriate for younger generations. Many kids today even *prefer* digital Hongbaos! --- ### 🏪 **If Physical Envelopes are Required (e.g., by family tradition):** - **Option 1: Buy pre-made Hongbaos** - Visit a ** nearby convenience store (7-Eleven, FamilyMart)** or **supermarket**— they often sell red envelopes year-round. - **Cost**: Usually ¥1–¥5 per envelope (or free with a small purchase). - **Time**: 5–10 minutes max. - **Option 2: DIY with red paper** - If no envelopes are available, cut ** red paper** (or use a red notebook cover, gift wrap, or even a red plastic bag) into a rectangle. Fold it into a simple envelope shape. - **Pro tip**: Write "恭喜" (Congratulations) or "新年快乐" on it to make it festive. - **Money tips**: - Use ** clean, uncrumpled bills** ( even if not "new"— it’s the gesture that counts!). - Avoid amounts with "4" (e.g., ¥40, ¥400). Stick to **¥50, ¥100, or ¥200** for younger cousins ( adjust based on your family’s norms). --- ### 💡 **If All else fails:** - **Explain the situation** to your cousins with a lighthearted message: > "Sorry I forgot to prepare physical Hongbaos! I’ll send you a digital one right now— hope you have a fun Chūnjié! 🧧" - **Give a small gift** (e.g., a candy, toy, or even a " lucky charm" like a red string bracelet) as a backup. - **Ask for help**: Text a family member: "Can you grab red envelopes for me at the store? I’ll pay you back!" --- ### 🌟 **Key takeaway:** **The gesture matters more than perfection**. In today’s world, digital Hongbaos are ** perfectly acceptable** ( even for traditional families), and most people will appreciate the effort. ** Act fast, stay calm, and focus on the joy of the celebration**— Chūnjié is about family, not the envelopes! **You’ve got this!** 🎉 *P.S. If you’re in a hurry, send digital Hongbaos first— then worry about physical envelopes later (or skip them altogether).* 😊

Scenario:
WIBTA if I told my cousin his kid can’t stay in our house? | My cousin (M27) recently moved in with my husband and I. We completely closed of the very large main bedroom and bathroom to create a flatlet for him that’s separate from the house with his own entrance so it’s basically two separate units of one house. Now my cousin has a 2 year old and he’s busy with a custody battle with his ex so he can get to spend more time with his son. I completely support this and really hopes he gets more time with his son. Yesterday my cousin came to ask me if it would be possible for my husband and I to convert our spare bedroom into a room for his son if and when he comes to visit over weekends. There is no access from my cousin’s room into our part of the house and he doesn’t have keys to come and go as he pleases. I understand that the court will be looking into his living situation to see if he has suitable space for his son to stay with him (and to be honest his current room and bathroom is more than big enough) but I’m not comfortable with letting his son sleep in our house if my cousin has no access to him and I’m not willing to take responsibility for his kid. The whole family is involved in this because that’s just the way my family is and everyone expects me to help out my cousin with his current custody situation to get him more time with his son. WIBTA for telling him I will not allow his son to sleep in our house and completely jeopardizing his court case?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **0 (Not an asshole)** **Here's why, step by step:** ### ✅ **You have every right to refuse** - **Boundaries are non-negotiable:** You’ve already made a *significant* accommodation by creating a ** separate, self-contained flatlet** for your cousin (with its own entrance, no shared access to your living space). This is more than most would do. - **"No access" is a critical issue:** If your cousin *cannot* freely enter your part of the house (e.g., no keys, no direct access), ** you cannot be responsible for his child’s safety** in your home. Courts *do* consider safety and supervision when evaluating living arrangements. If the child is in your space without your cousin having access to them (e.g., if he’s in a meeting or work), ** you’d be legally liable** for any accidents or emergencies. - **The spare room request is *not* necessary for the custody case:** You explicitly state his current flatlet is "more than big enough" for the child. Courts assess ** the primary caregiver’s *own* living space**— not whether extended family *could* host the child. If his flatlet meets basic standards (which it does), the court won’t penalize him for not using *your* spare room. ### ❌ **Why the family pressure is misplaced** - **"The whole family expects me to help" is not a valid reason to overextend yourself.** You’re not obligated to sacrifice your own boundaries, safety, or peace of mind for others’ expectations. - **"Jeopardizing his court case" is a misunderstanding:** Courts don’t require extended family to host children. They evaluate the *primary caregiver’s* ability to provide a stable, safe environment *in their own home*. If his flatlet is adequate (as you described), ** your refusal does *not* harm his case**— it’s irrelevant to the court’s assessment. ### 💡 **What you *should* do** - **Firmly but compassionately say:** > "I’m so glad you’re fighting for time with your son, and I’m proud of you. I’ve already set up the flatlet to give you a stable space for him, and I’m happy to support that. But I can’t have his son stay in *our* house because I’m not comfortable with the lack of access to him, and I don’t want to be responsible for his safety when you’re not here. I hope you understand this is about boundaries, not about not wanting to help." - **Redirect the family pressure:** > "This is my home, and my husband and I need to prioritize our own safety and comfort. I’m supporting him in the ways I can (the flatlet), but I won’t overextend myself. I hope we can all respect that." ### 🌟 **Final verdict** **You are absolutely not an asshole.** - Setting boundaries around your home, safety, and liability is ** healthy and responsible**. - Courts *do not* require extended family to host children for custody cases. - Refusing this request **does not jeopardize his case**— it’s a non-issue for the court. - **You’ve already done more than enough.** Prioritize your own well-being. > * "You can’t pour from an empty cup. Protecting your own space isn’t selfish—it’s necessary."* 💛 > *P.S. If the family continues to pressure you, remind them: "This is my home. I’m supporting my cousin in the ways I can, but I won’t compromise my own boundaries."*
